batchName: Empire: Augustus and the Principate (27 BC-AD 14) - Medium Batch 2
chapterName: Empire: Augustus and the Principate (27 BC-AD 14)

questions.question: How do most modern historians describe the Principate?
options: As a true partnership with the Senate
As rule by the army alone
questions.explanation: A 19th-century German scholar called it a genuine partnership between emperor and Senate, but most modern historians reject that view.
questions.sourceQuote: Most modern historians reject that, calling it monarchy in disguise.

questions.question: Who secretly organised the Germanic alliance that destroyed the Roman legions in AD 9?
options: A Parthian general sent to Germany
A Cherusci chieftain raised as a hostage in Rome
A Gallic king from beyond the Alps
questions.explanation: The chieftain had served as a Roman officer and was the governor's trusted adviser. He fed the governor false reports of a revolt.
questions.sourceQuote: His trusted adviser was a Germanic chieftain of the Cherusci tribe who had been raised as a hostage in Rome and served as a Roman officer.

questions.question: What happened to Egypt after Octavian conquered it?
options: It was split among the legions
It was given to Antony's children
It was left as an allied kingdom
It was ruled by the Senate
questions.explanation: Egypt's treasure paid off Octavian's war debts. Senators were even forbidden to travel there.
questions.sourceQuote: Egypt became Octavian's personal property, and its treasure paid off his war debts.

questions.question: Who built the first Pantheon in Rome?
questions.explanation: Agrippa, Augustus's old friend and admiral, also took charge of the water supply, drains, public baths and roads.
questions.sourceQuote: Agrippa, his old friend and admiral, took charge of the water supply, drains, public baths and roads, and built the first Pantheon.

questions.question: Roughly how many legions came with the "troubled" provinces Augustus agreed to govern in 27 BC?
questions.explanation: The provinces included Spain, Gaul, Syria and Egypt, with about twenty legions. The Senate kept only five or six.
questions.sourceQuote: These happened to include Spain, Gaul, Syria and Egypt, and with them about twenty legions.

questions.question: How did Augustus reform tax collection in the provinces?
options: He made the army collect the taxes
He sold collection rights to private companies
He used salaried collectors instead of private companies
He let each governor keep the taxes
questions.explanation: Under the Republic, private companies bought the right to collect taxes and squeezed the provinces. Augustus used censuses to fix each province's share.
questions.sourceQuote: Augustus replaced them with salaried collectors, using censuses to fix each province's share.

questions.question: Which power, granted for life, let Augustus summon assemblies, propose laws and veto any decision?
questions.explanation: Tribunician power was the authority of the ancient tribunes who protected ordinary citizens. Greater proconsular power, by contrast, made him superior to every governor.
questions.sourceQuote: It let him summon the Senate and the people's assemblies, propose laws, and veto any decision.

questions.question: After marching on Rome in 43 BC, at what age did Octavian become consul?
questions.explanation: He used Caesar's money and his own to win over veterans and raise a private army, then became consul at just 19.
questions.sourceQuote: He used Caesar's money and his own to win over the dead dictator's veterans, raised a private army, and in 43 BC marched on Rome, becoming consul at just 19.

questions.question: What did the Senate wish each new emperor in later Roman times?
questions.explanation: Later Romans were kinder to Augustus than his contemporaries. A legal scholar of his own day had mourned the lost liberty of the Republic.
questions.sourceQuote: Later Romans were kinder: the Senate wished each new emperor to be "more fortunate than Augustus".

questions.question: What service did the vigiles, created by Augustus in AD 6, provide for Rome?
questions.explanation: The vigiles had seven units covering fourteen city districts. A permanent official for the grain supply followed in AD 8.
questions.sourceQuote: For the capital he created a combined fire brigade and night police (*vigiles*) in AD 6, with seven units covering fourteen city districts.
